unit.title: Why pushing feels different from pulling a lever
unit.needIt: Your sense of right and wrong often fires before you think, and reasons arrive later to defend it. Knowing that helps you tell a principle from a flinch.
unit.why: People often feel that pushing a man to stop a train is wrong, but turning a track to save five people is right. Scientists found that our brains use different systems for these choices. One system uses logic while the other reacts with raw emotion.
unit.outcome: Identify when your moral gut feeling might be a shortcut rather than a logical conclusion.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you make a quick choice at a store or judge a person's actions on social media. It happens whenever you feel a strong 'no' without being able to explain why.
unit.do: Next time you feel a strong moral judgment, stop and ask yourself if you are reacting to a fact or just a feeling.

quiz.q: What is the main difference in the bystander case versus the fat man case?
quiz.why: Thompson suggests that the fat man case involves a violation of an individual's right.
quiz.quote: The notion of a right is what prohibits killing the one in the fat man case.

quiz.q: What is the main difference in the bystander case versus the fat man case?
quiz.why: The lecture explains that people see these as having different moral mandates.
quiz.quote: The difference between our response to Fat Man and our response to Bystander, says Thompson in that 1985 article, is one that we should respect.

quiz.q: What is a 'confabulation' in the context of human reasoning?
quiz.why: Green notes that people often make up reasons for choices their brains already made.
quiz.quote: So famously, people are more likely to choose an object that lies on the left-hand side of a visual array than an object that lies on the right-hand side of that visual array.

quiz.q: According to Josh Green, why do we often struggle to explain our moral feelings?
choices: Our motivations are opaque to us
We are not thinking at all
quiz.why: Green argues that our brains often make decisions based on feelings we aren't even aware of.
quiz.quote: So there are many cases, Green points out, where our motivations are opaque to us, where we think we're responding to one thing, but in fact we're responding to else.

quiz.why: Sunstein defines heuristics as tools for dealing with complex worlds quickly.
quiz.quote: Heuristics are fast and frugal tools for dealing with the complexity of the world when we're faced with time sensitive decision-making tasks.

quiz.q: What does Sunstein say about the relationship between target and heuristic attributes?
choices: They are only for non-moral cases
quiz.why: He explains that these attributes usually match up, which is why the shortcuts work so well in daily life.
quiz.quote: Target and heuristic attributes generally coincide. That's how the heuristic attributes came to be the ones which you're using as the markers of the target.

choices: How easy it is to think of cases
quiz.why: It is the tendency to judge likelihood based on how easily examples come to mind.
quiz.quote: That's a heuristic that says, look, I'm trying to figure out likely something is to happen, and here's a good way to determine how likely something is to happen. I think about how easy it is for me to think of cases where that did happen.

Our brains use shortcuts called heuristics.
